newsitem.title: UK: Europe rates to stay low but UK signals new cycle.
newsitem.headline: Europe rates to stay low but UK signals new cycle.

text.p: Economies in continental Europe are too weak to warrant the monetary tightening witnessed in Britain this week and even the United States may not follow suit for some time, analysts said on Thursday.

Nevertheless, the British rate rise heralds a turning point for the rate cycle in Europe. While rates are unlikely to move higher soon, heavyweight economies such as Germany and its satellites have seen the end of the cuts, analysts said.
"The UK is really a leading indicator of what is to come -- not in the near term but towards the end of next year," said Keith Edmonds, chief analyst at IBJ international in London.

"Growth in Europe is starting to revive. In a number of countries it appears the monetary authorities aren't going to be cutting interest rates anymore but neither are they at the stage of thinking seriously about raising rates," he said.
Britain surprised financial markets on Wednesday with a 1/4 point rise in interest rates, bringing the base rate to six percent. It was the first rise since February 1995.

With consumer spending blooming, shops bustling and sterling flying high, the rise was seen as a shrewd move by Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Kenneth Clarke to curb inflation before it got out of hand.

Economic growth in Britain was at 2.3 percent in the third quarter and set to push toward four percent in 1997. Meanwhile, the core rate of inflation at 2.9 percent is already beyond the government's 2.5 percent target.

But the picture is very different in the rest of Europe. Germany managed growth of 1.5 percent in the second quarter while economies in France and Italy are still contracting. Consumer inflation is virtually nonexistant.

France on Thursday actually cut its intervention rate by five basis points to 3.20 percent, the 10th cut this year, just after it reported unemployment hit a record high of 12.6 percent in September. Italy, Spain and Sweden are thought likely to see further interest rate falls.
Analysts said Britain's economy and interest rate cycle has been out of synch with the rest of Europe since the pound left the Exchange Rate Mechanism in September 1992.

"We haven't really seen the sharp kind of fiscal consolidation we've seen in other countries," said IBJ's Edmonds. "Our trade pattern is now split more evenly with continental countries and the U.S. so we've benefitted from the surge in U.S. growth to a greater extent."
There were signs of life, however, in some of the European countries, particularly Germany and Denmark.
"We are starting to look at core Europe with a little more nervousness on short-term interest rates," Francesco Giordano, senior economist at San Paolo Bank in London, said.
"Recent declarations from Bundesbank officials suggested quite clearly that there is a clear changing bias towards neutrality at best from easing," he said.
He did not expect an interest rate increase in Germany until the third quarter of 1997.

Edmonds said the next countries to raise rates would likely be those that have cut agressively like the mark bloc, which includes Belgium and the Netherlands. The Netherlands special advances rate at 2.50 percent is equal to Germany's discount rate and below Germany's three percent repo rate. He, too, did not expect Germany's rates to move up.
There was more speculation about U.S. interest rates, though opinion was divided.
Edmonds said the case for a modest interest rate rise in the first quarter of 1997 will become overhwhelming.

Steven Bell, chief economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London, sees the Federal Reserve on hold for a year. Unlike in Britain, consumer spending in the United States remains in check, he said. Personal spending in September rose a slim 0.1 percent or $3.4 billion, Commerce Department data on Thursday showed.
"The movement in bond yields helped stimulate the economy when it was slowing over the winter and helped choke off the surge in the second quarter," he said.
